title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
summary: An original fable about a thirsty crow who outsmarts a scheming fox by dropping pebbles into a jar to raise the water instead of falling for his trick.
poll: Being clever and patient will always work better than trying to trick someone.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
A crow was thirsty. She found a jar with water in it. But the water was down low. She could not reach it with her beak.

A fox came by. He said, 'I can help you. Tip the jar. The water will spill out. Then you can drink it fast.' This was a trick. The fox wanted the water for himself.

The crow did not trust the fox. If the water spilled on the sand, it would soak in fast. No one would get a good drink.

The crow had a clever plan. She saw small pebbles on the ground. She dropped one pebble into the jar. Then she dropped another. The water moved up a little bit each time.

She dropped pebble after pebble. The water rose to the top. The crow drank the water at last!

The fox got no water. His trick did not work. The crow's patience and clever plan had won.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
One hot day, a crow felt very thirsty. She found a tall jar with water inside. But the water was near the bottom. Her beak could not reach it.

A fox walked by and saw her trying. 'I can help you,' said the fox with a sly smile. 'Just tip the jar. The water will spill on the sand. Then we can both drink.' This sounded nice. But it was really a trick.

The crow did not trust the fox. If the water spilled on the sand, it would soak in fast. No one would get a good drink.

Instead, the crow had a clever plan. She saw small pebbles near the jar. One by one, she dropped them inside. Each pebble made the water rise a little higher.

She kept dropping pebbles. At last the water reached the top. The thirsty crow could drink!

The fox walked away with no water. His trick had failed. The crow's patience and clever plan had won the day.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
One hot afternoon, a crow felt very thirsty as she flew over the dry land. She found a tall clay jar with a little water at the bottom. She landed by it and dipped in her beak. But the water was too far down to reach.

A fox was passing by and saw the crow trying hard. 'I can help you,' the fox said with a sly grin. 'Just tip the jar on its side. The water will spill on the sand, and we can share it.' It sounded kind. But it was really just a clever trick.

The crow thought about it first. She knew that water spilled on dry sand would soak in fast, and neither of them would get a good drink. She said no to the fox.

Instead, the crow came up with her own clever plan. She saw small pebbles near the jar. One by one, she picked them up and dropped them inside. With each pebble, the water rose a little higher.

She kept dropping pebbles until the water reached the top. At last, the thirsty crow drank her fill.

The fox left without a single drop of water. His trick had failed. The crow's patience and clever thinking had won the day.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
One scorching afternoon, as the sun beat down on the dry savanna, a crow felt very thirsty. Flying low, she spotted a tall clay jar under a thorn tree. A little water sat at the bottom, but it was far too low for her beak to reach.

A fox was prowling nearby and noticed the crow struggling. 'Let me help you,' the fox said with a sly grin. 'Just tip the jar on its side. The water will spill onto the sand, and we can share it as friends.' It sounded generous. But it was really just a clever trick to get the water for himself.

The crow thought about the offer carefully. She knew that water spilled onto dry sand would soak in almost at once, leaving neither of them a good drink. The quick fox would likely grab whatever was left. She firmly said no.

Instead, the crow came up with her own clever plan. She noticed small pebbles scattered near the jar. One by one, she picked them up and dropped them inside. With each pebble, the water rose a little higher toward the rim.

Patiently, she kept dropping pebbles until the water reached the very top. At last, the thirsty crow drank her fill, feeling proud of her own cleverness.

The fox slunk away without a drop of water, grumbling under his breath. His trick had failed completely. The crow's patience, not his tricky scheme, had won the day.

The crow stops to think. She knows that water spilled on dry sand soaks in almost at once, so neither of them would get a good drink. She firmly says no to the fox.

Determined to solve the problem herself, the crow looks around. She sees small pebbles scattered near the jar. One by one, she drops them into the jar. Each pebble makes the water rise a little higher.

She stays patient, dropping pebble after pebble, even though the work is slow. After many trips, the water finally rises high enough to reach.

At last, the crow drinks and feels satisfied. The fox, meanwhile, walks away with no water at all. His scheme has failed completely against the crow's patience and determined effort.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
Picture a crow who is very thirsty, flying over the dry, sun-baked ground of a wide savanna. At last, she spots a tall clay jar sitting in the thin shade of a thorn tree. A shallow pool of water rests at the bottom, but it sits much too low for her beak to reach, no matter how she tries.

A fox is prowling nearby and notices the crow struggling. He already has an idea, but it is really a hidden scheme of his own. 'Let me help you,' he offers smoothly. 'Just tip the jar onto its side. The water will spill out onto the sand, and we can share it together.' It sounds kind, but underneath, the fox only wants the water for himself.

The crow pauses to think it over. She knows that water spilled on dry sand soaks in almost instantly, so neither animal would get a good drink, and the quick fox would likely grab whatever was left first. She firmly declines his offer.

Determined to solve the problem on her own, the crow looks around the ground nearby. She notices a scattering of small pebbles in the dust. One by one, she picks up each pebble and drops it carefully into the jar. Every pebble makes the water rise a little higher toward the rim.

She stays patient despite the slow, tiring work, dropping pebble after pebble, trip after trip, even as her wings grow heavy. Eventually, after many trips, the water finally rises high enough for her to reach.

At last, the crow drinks deeply and feels fully satisfied with her own clever thinking. The fox, meanwhile, slinks away with no water at all, his scheme having failed completely against the crow's quiet patience and determined persistence.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
Picture a crow who is desperately thirsty, flying across the dry, sun-baked Arabian savanna in search of water. At last, her sharp eyes spot a tall clay jar resting in the thin shade of a thorn tree. A shallow pool of water rests at the very bottom, but it sits far too low for her beak to reach.

A fox is prowling nearby and notices the crow struggle with the jar. He already has a quiet scheme in mind. 'Let me help you,' he offers smoothly, his eyes gleaming. 'Just tip the jar onto its side, and the water will spill out where we can share it together.' The offer sounds kind on the surface. But underneath, it is really a clever scheme meant to claim the water for himself.

The crow pauses to think it over carefully. Spilled water on dry sand soaks in almost instantly, leaving nothing behind for either of them. The quick fox, she knows, would likely snatch up whatever puddle remained first. Firmly, she declines his offer.

Determined to solve the problem through her own wits, the crow looks around and notices a scattering of small pebbles lying in the dust nearby. One by one, she picks up each pebble and drops it into the jar. With every pebble that sinks, the water level rises a little higher toward the rim.

She stays patient despite the slow and tiring progress, dropping pebble after pebble, trip after trip, never giving up even as her wings grow heavy with fatigue. Eventually, after many trips back and forth, the water finally rises high enough for her to reach comfortably.

At last, the crow drinks deeply and feels fully satisfied, both by the cool water and by the quiet success of her own clever thinking. The fox, meanwhile, slinks away empty-handed and clearly annoyed, his scheme having failed completely against the crow's patience and steady determination.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
Picture a crow who is desperately thirsty, flying across the dry, sun-baked Arabian savanna in search of any source of water. At last, her sharp eyes spot a tall clay jar resting in the thin shade of a solitary thorn tree. A shallow pool of water rests at its very bottom, but it sits far too low for her beak to reach, no matter how she angles her head.

A fox is prowling nearby and notices the crow struggle with the jar. He already has a quiet scheme in mind. 'Let me help you,' he says smoothly, his eyes gleaming. 'Just tip the jar onto its side, and the water will spill out onto the sand where we can share it together.' The offer sounds kind on the surface, but underneath, it is really a clever scheme meant to claim the water for himself alone.

The crow pauses to think it over carefully, weighing the fox's words against what she already knows about the desert. She understands that precious water spilled on sun-baked sand soaks in almost instantly, leaving nothing behind for either of them to drink, and that the quick fox would likely snatch up whatever puddle remained first. Firmly, without the slightest hesitation, she declines his offer.

Determined to solve the problem through her own wits rather than trust a stranger's scheme, the crow looks around and notices a scattering of small pebbles lying half buried in the dust nearby. One by one, she picks up each pebble in her beak and drops it carefully into the narrow opening of the jar. With every pebble that sinks, the water level rises a little higher toward the rim.

She stays patient despite the slow and exhausting progress, dropping pebble after pebble, trip after tiring trip, never giving up even as her wings grow heavy with fatigue and the afternoon wears on. Eventually, after many trips back and forth across the sand, the water finally rises high enough for her to reach it comfortably.

At last, the crow drinks deeply and feels fully satisfied, both by the cool water and by the quiet success of her own clever thinking. The fox, meanwhile, slinks away empty-handed and clearly annoyed, his scheme having failed completely against the crow's patience, her careful planning, and her steady determination to solve the problem herself.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
Beneath a hot midday sun that bears down on the dry Arabian savanna, a thirsty crow searches tirelessly for water, her need growing with each passing hour of the long afternoon. At last, her sharp eyes find a tall clay jar resting in the shade of a thorn tree, with a little water visible at the bottom. She lands beside it and dips in her beak, but the water sits too low to reach, no matter how she tilts her head against the narrow opening.

A fox is prowling nearby, looking for his own drink, and he notices the crow's trouble. He offers a plan meant to deceive her, calculating that she will not see through it. 'Let me help you,' he says smoothly, though his intentions are far from kind. 'If you tip the jar onto its side, the water will spill across the sand, and we can share it.' The plan sounds reasonable, yet it is really a deceptive scheme to get the water for the fox alone, since the sand would soak up most of it at once, and his greater speed would let him grab whatever is left before the crow could even land.

Seeing through the deception right away, the crow turns down the offer without a moment's hesitation. She knows that spilled water would vanish into the ground before either of them could drink enough, and that trusting the fox's scheme would leave her worse off than before.

Determined to rely on her own ingenious thinking instead, the crow notices small pebbles scattered near the jar. One by one, she drops them into the narrow opening, watching with quiet satisfaction as the water rises little by little with every addition.

Her persistence never wavers, even though the task takes many tiring trips in the relentless heat. At last, her patient work pays off: the water rises high enough, and she drinks deeply and triumphantly, having solved with her mind what trickery never could.

Realizing his scheme to outwit the crow has failed completely, the fox slinks away without a drop of water, having underestimated the quiet power of patience and ingenious thought.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
Beneath a hot midday sun beating down relentlessly on the vast, dry Arabian savanna, a thirsty crow searches tirelessly and with mounting desperation for any accessible source of water, her need growing with each sweltering, seemingly endless hour. At last, her sharp eyes find a tall clay jar resting within the thin, inadequate shade of a solitary thorn tree, with a little water faintly visible near the bottom. She lands beside it at once and dips in her beak, but the water sits too low to reach, no matter how she tilts her head against the jar's stubbornly narrow neck.

A fox is prowling the surrounding area, looking for his own refreshment, and he notices the crow's evident trouble. He offers a plan carefully and deliberately calculated to deceive her. 'Allow me to help you,' he offers smoothly, though his underlying intentions remain far from kind or sincere. 'If you tip the jar onto its side, the water will spill across the sand, and we can share it together as companions.' The plan sounds entirely reasonable, even admirably kind, yet it is really a deceptive scheme to secure the water exclusively for the fox himself, since he understands perfectly well that the sand would soak up most of it almost instantly, and his own considerably greater speed would let him grab whatever remains before the slower crow could even manage to land.

Seeing through the deception immediately and without the slightest doubt, the crow turns down the offer without a moment's hesitation. She reasons, through simple yet entirely sound logic, that spilled water would vanish into the ground long before either creature could drink a genuinely satisfying amount, and that trusting the fox's elaborate scheme would leave her considerably worse off than her present, already difficult circumstance.

Determined to rely exclusively on her own ingenious thinking instead of the fox's hollow and self-serving promises, the crow notices small pebbles strewn near the jar's base. One by one, she drops them carefully into the narrow opening, observing with quiet, steadily growing satisfaction as the water level rises a little higher with each successive addition.

Her persistence never once wavers, even though the repetitive task takes dozens of exhausting trips beneath the unforgiving desert heat. At last, her patient and remarkably methodical work pays off: the water rises nearly to the rim, and she drinks deeply and triumphantly, having solved through sheer intellect alone a problem that deceptive trickery could never possibly have resolved.

Realizing at last that his elaborate scheme to outwit the crow has failed entirely and irreversibly, the fox slinks away without a single drop of water to show for his considerable efforts, having gravely underestimated the formidable power of patience combined with genuinely ingenious thought.

versions.title: The Clever Fox and the Thirsty Crow
versions.text:
A thirsty crow, driven by mounting desperation beneath the merciless midday sun of the parched Arabian savanna, eventually discovered a tall clay jar resting in the thin shade of a solitary thorn tree, its shallow pool of water frustratingly visible yet entirely unreachable given the vessel's stubbornly narrow neck, regardless of how she angled her beak against its rim. A fox, prowling nearby in search of his own refreshment, noticed her evident struggle and approached with a proposal deliberately calculated to deceive: he suggested that she simply tip the jar onto its side so the water might spill across the sand for them to share, a plan that sounded generous on its surface but was, in truth, a self-serving scheme designed to secure the water for himself alone, since he understood that the thirsty ground would absorb most of it almost instantly and that his own considerable speed would let him claim whatever remained before the comparatively slower crow could even land.

Recognizing this deception without hesitation, the crow declined the offer, reasoning that spilled water would simply vanish into the parched earth before either creature could drink a meaningful amount, leaving her in a worse position than before. Determined instead to rely entirely on her own ingenious reasoning, she surveyed her surroundings, noticed a scattering of small pebbles near the jar's base, and began methodically dropping them one by one into the narrow opening, watching with quiet satisfaction as the water level rose incrementally with each addition.

Her persistence never wavered throughout the repetitive, physically demanding task, which required dozens of exhausting trips beneath the unforgiving heat before the water finally rose high enough for her to drink deeply and triumphantly, having solved through sheer intellect a problem that brute strength or deceptive trickery could never have resolved. The fox, recognizing that his scheme to outwit the crow had failed completely, slunk away without a single drop of water, having gravely underestimated the formidable combination of patience and ingenious thought.

This small desert drama illustrates a lesson that extends well beyond its two animal characters: cleverness paired with persistence will reliably outlast shortcuts built on deception, however smoothly those shortcuts may be presented. The crow never matched the fox's speed, cunning reputation, or confident charm, yet she required none of these qualities, since a patient mind willing to solve a problem step by step proved entirely sufficient to secure what pure trickery could never deliver.

a loud warning call given to other animals
questions.why: The fox's offer was really a scheme, a secret plan meant to get the water for himself.

wrong.A: A scheme is not a kind favor.
wrong.B: A scheme is not a container.
wrong.D: A scheme is not a sound.

questions.stem: Why would spilling the water onto the sand not have helped either animal?
options: The jar would shatter and cut both of their feet on the hot sand
The fox would simply refuse to share any spilled water with the crow
The hot sun would somehow turn the water into solid ice on the sand
The sand would absorb the water quickly, leaving little to drink
questions.why: Dry sand soaks up water almost instantly, so very little would be left for either animal to drink.

wrong.A: The story never mentions a broken jar.
wrong.B: The issue is the sand, not the fox refusing to share.
wrong.C: The desert heat would not freeze water.

questions.stem: What does the fox's offer to 'help' most likely reveal about his true goal?
options: He wanted to get the water for himself before the crow could
He simply wanted to prove he was a truly kind animal
He only wanted to learn exactly how crows like to drink
He merely wanted to test whether the old jar was heavy
questions.why: Because the fox was faster, spilling the water would let him grab it before the crow could drink any.

wrong.B: His plan was not truly about kindness.
wrong.C: Learning about crows is not his goal.
wrong.D: Testing the jar's weight is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What was the result of the crow dropping pebble after pebble into the jar?
options: The old clay jar suddenly cracked and leaked out
The fox finally agreed to share his own water
The water slowly rose until she could reach it
The small pebbles quietly dissolved inside the water
questions.why: Each pebble took up space in the jar, which caused the water level to rise.

wrong.A: The jar did not crack.
wrong.B: The fox never shared any water.
wrong.D: Pebbles do not dissolve in water.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing three very different deserts around the world and their weather
In the order the crow faces a problem, rejects a trick, and solves it herself
By simply listing facts about foxes and crows in general, one after another
By jumping back and forth between two completely unrelated stories about birds
questions.why: The story follows the crow from discovering the problem, to rejecting the fox's scheme, to solving it with pebbles.

wrong.A: Only one desert setting is described.
wrong.C: The story is a narrative, not a list of facts.
wrong.D: There is only one connected story, told in order.

MID.prompt: Explain why the fox's plan would not have worked, and explain how the crow's plan was better. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained why the fox's plan would fail.
I explained why the crow's plan worked.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: The fox's plan would not have worked because spilling the water onto the dry sand would let it soak in almost instantly, and the quick fox would snatch any that was left before the crow could drink. The crow's plan was better because she dropped pebbles into the jar one by one, which slowly raised the water without wasting a single drop. Her patience and determination let her solve the problem on her own, while the fox's scheme would have left both animals thirsty.

keyWords.definition: very clever and original, especially in solving a problem
keyWords.example: The engineer designed an ingenious bridge that needed no support pillars.

keyWords.definition: a great success or victory, often after difficulty
keyWords.example: The team celebrated their triumph after months of hard training.

keyWords.definition: to defeat someone by being smarter or more clever than them
keyWords.example: The chess player outwitted her opponent with a surprising final move.

keyWords.definition: continuing to try something despite difficulty
keyWords.example: Her persistence in practicing the violin finally paid off at the concert.

keyWords.definition: to make someone believe something that is not true
keyWords.example: The advertisement tried to deceive customers about the product's real price.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A crow's patient, ingenious reasoning lets her outwit a fox's deceptive scheme
A fox's clever trick helps a thirsty crow find water much faster
Two desert animals work together to build a brand new water source
A fox carefully explains the chemistry of evaporation in the open desert
questions.why: The story shows the crow using patient, ingenious reasoning to get the water while seeing through the fox's deceptive scheme.

wrong.B: The fox's trick does not help the crow; she rejects it.
wrong.C: The two animals do not cooperate.
wrong.D: No scientific explanation of evaporation appears.

questions.stem: What exactly did the fox propose, and what was his real motive?
options: He proposed digging a well, intending to keep it hidden from the crow
He proposed flying together to find a new jar, intending to abandon the crow midair
He proposed tipping the jar, intending to claim most of the spilled water himself
He proposed sharing his own water, intending to ask for a favor later
questions.why: The fox suggested tipping the jar, knowing his speed would let him claim the spilled water before the crow could.

wrong.A: No well is dug in the story.
wrong.B: The fox and crow never fly anywhere together.
wrong.D: The fox has no water of his own to share.

questions.stem: In the story, the word ingenious most nearly means —
options: loud and demanding toward other animals
cautious and fearful of almost everything
slow and careless about small details
cleverly original in solving a problem
questions.why: The crow's ingenious reasoning refers to her original, clever way of solving the water problem with pebbles.

wrong.A: Ingenious does not describe volume or demands.
wrong.B: Ingenious is not about fear.
wrong.C: Ingenious describes cleverness, not slowness.

questions.stem: Why does the fox's plan reveal more cunning than kindness?
options: He offers a solution that conveniently benefits only himself once examined closely
He never actually speaks one single word to the crow, so the crow ignores him
He immediately runs far away without proposing anything at all, and the crow is left alone
He simply asks the crow to teach him how to fly like a bird, which costs him nothing
questions.why: Once the sand's absorption and the fox's speed are considered, his 'helpful' plan actually benefits only him.

wrong.B: The fox does speak directly to the crow.
wrong.C: The fox does propose a plan rather than leaving.
wrong.D: The fox never asks to be taught to fly.

questions.stem: What does the crow's choice to reject the fox's offer suggest about her character?
options: She is impulsive and acts without ever thinking things through
She is reasoned and skeptical of offers that seem too convenient
She is deeply afraid of foxes and most other animals
She prefers clever tricks over slow, patient solutions
questions.why: The crow carefully reasons through the fox's offer before rejecting it, showing thoughtful skepticism rather than fear or impulsiveness.

wrong.A: She pauses to think carefully rather than acting on impulse.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests general fear of foxes.
wrong.D: She rejects a trick in favor of her own patient solution.

questions.stem: What is the underlying reason spilling the water would have failed both animals?
options: Clay jars simply cannot be tipped over by small birds, so the water would not spill
The fox was, in truth, actually quite afraid of water, and would not go near any puddle
Dry sand absorbs liquid rapidly, and the faster fox would reach any surviving puddle first
The jar's water had already been badly contaminated by the desert wind and dust
questions.why: Rapid absorption by the sand, combined with the fox's greater speed, meant spilling would leave little or nothing for the crow.

wrong.A: The jar's weight is never discussed as a barrier.
wrong.B: The fox shows no fear of water.
wrong.D: Contamination is never mentioned.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly reflects the order of events?
options: The crow drinks the water, the fox proposes tipping it, then she finds pebbles
The crow drops in pebbles, the fox proposes tipping it, then she drinks
The fox leaves at once, the crow finds the jar, then she drinks
The fox proposes tipping the jar, the crow declines, she drops pebbles, then drinks
questions.why: The fox proposes his scheme first, the crow declines it, then she drops pebbles, and finally she drinks.

wrong.A: Drinking happens only after the pebbles raise the water, not before.
wrong.B: The fox proposes his plan before the crow drops any pebbles.
wrong.C: The fox leaves only after his scheme fails, not at the start.

questions.stem: Why does the author have the fox fail completely rather than partly succeed?
options: To make the ending more exciting with a loud, dramatic chase
To suggest that foxes in general cannot be trusted near jars
To emphasize decisively that deception offers no advantage over patient ingenuity
To carefully explain the traditional process of manufacturing clay jars
questions.why: A complete failure for the fox makes the fable's lesson unmistakable: deception gains nothing against patient, clever thinking.

wrong.A: No chase scene occurs in the story.
wrong.B: The lesson is about behavior, not jars specifically.
wrong.D: The story never explains jar manufacturing.

HIGH.prompt: The story's moral is that cleverness and patience beat trickery. Do you agree this is true in real life, not just in fables? Support your argument with evidence from the story and address a counterargument.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the moral.
I supported my position with evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one counterargument.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that cleverness and patience usually beat trickery in the long run. In the story, the fox's deceptive scheme completely failed because it relied on circumstances that actually favored him, while the crow's ingenious, patient plan with the pebbles worked exactly as she intended. Someone might argue that tricks sometimes succeed because they can surprise a victim before they have time to think. However, as the story shows, a careful thinker who pauses to consider an offer, as the crow did, is often able to see through deception and find a more reliable solution on her own.

LOW.stem: Where does the crow find the small pebbles?
options: Up in a tree
In the fox's paw
On the ground
Inside the jar
LOW.why: The text says the crow saw small pebbles on the ground.

wrong.A: The pebbles are not in a tree.
wrong.B: The fox does not hold any pebbles.
wrong.D: The crow drops the pebbles into the jar; they begin on the ground.

LOW.stem: Why does the fox get no water?
options: His trick does not work.
The crow gives it away.
He is too small to drink.
He falls asleep first.
LOW.why: The text says the fox got no water because his trick did not work.

wrong.B: The crow drinks the water herself.
wrong.C: The text does not say the fox is too small.
wrong.D: The fox does not fall asleep.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word patience means —
options: being loud when you are upset
wanting a thing right away
giving up when it is hard
staying calm and not giving up
LOW.why: The crow keeps dropping pebble after pebble, calmly, until the water rises.

wrong.A: The crow is not loud or upset.
wrong.B: The crow waits and works step by step.
wrong.C: The crow does not give up.

LOW.stem: How is the crow different from the fox?
options: The crow is bigger and louder.
The crow solves it on her own.
The crow wants to trick him.
The crow has a jar of her own.
LOW.why: The fox tries a trick, but the crow uses pebbles to solve the problem herself.

wrong.A: Size and loudness are not mentioned.
wrong.C: The fox is the one who plays a trick.
wrong.D: The jar is just something the crow finds.

MID.stem: Where does the crow find the tall clay jar?
options: On top of a high stone wall
In the shade of a thorn tree
Beside a deep, cold river
Inside a dark, damp cave
MID.why: The text says the jar is in the shade of a thorn tree.

wrong.A: A wall is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The ground is dry, and no river is near.
wrong.D: No cave is in the story.

MID.stem: In the story, the word determined means —
options: easily tired out
unsure what to do
firm about not giving up
glad to share with others
MID.why: The crow is determined to solve the problem and keeps dropping pebbles even though it is slow.

wrong.A: The crow keeps working for many trips.
wrong.B: The crow has a clear plan.
wrong.D: The crow refuses to share by tipping the jar.

MID.stem: What does the crow's choice to solve the problem herself show about her?
options: She is clever and hard-working.
She is lazy and not so clever.
She is afraid of the strong fox.
She is angry at the hot sun.
MID.why: She thinks of the pebble plan and makes many trips to carry it out.

wrong.B: She works through many slow trips.
wrong.C: She says no to the fox firmly.
wrong.D: The text does not say she is angry.

MID.stem: Why does the author tell about the pebbles one by one over many trips?
options: To show the jar is very large
To tell how many pebbles she has
To explain why the sun is so hot
To show the plan needs patience
MID.why: The author shows the crow dropping pebble after pebble to show that her plan is slow and takes patience.

wrong.A: The jar is tall, but that is not the point of the repeated trips.
wrong.B: The text gives no count of pebbles.
wrong.C: The sun is only part of the setting.

HIGH.stem: What makes it hard for the crow to drink at first?
options: The jar is full of sand.
The jar has a cover on top.
The thorn tree blocks the jar.
The water sits too low to reach.
HIGH.why: The text says the water is too low to reach, even with her head tilted at the narrow opening.

wrong.A: The jar holds water, not sand.
wrong.B: No cover is mentioned.
wrong.C: The tree gives shade; it does not block the jar.

HIGH.stem: The passage says her persistence never wavers. What does persistence most nearly mean?
options: refusing to give up
feeling very hot and tired
asking for help
moving very fast
HIGH.why: She keeps making tiring trips in the heat without stopping, so persistence means refusing to give up.

wrong.B: The heat is hot, but persistence is about effort.
wrong.C: She keeps working on her own.
wrong.D: The word is about not quitting, not speed.

HIGH.stem: What effect does each pebble have on the water in the jar?
options: It makes the water muddy.
It makes the water rise a little.
It makes the water dry up.
It makes the water spill out.
HIGH.why: The text says the water rises little by little with every pebble added.

wrong.A: Muddy water is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The water rises, so it does not dry up.
wrong.D: The water stays in the jar as it rises.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author describe the many tiring trips she makes in the heat?
options: To show the jar is far away
To show the fox is faster
To show real effort by the crow
To show the sun was setting
HIGH.why: The tiring trips show that the crow's success came from real patient effort.

wrong.A: The jar is beside the crow, not far away.
wrong.B: The fox fails and slinks away.
wrong.D: The scene is in the midday heat, not sunset.
